# Nitroglycerin and dynamite (`nitroglycerin_dynamite`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: needs nitric_acid, sulphuric_acid; helped by soap, gunpowder
- Core idea: Nitroglycerin is a shock-sensitive liquid whose detonation sends a shock wave through rock. Early civil engineers used it for blasting, but transport and handling caused fatal accidents. Nobel’s dynamite held the liquid in an absorbent solid. This made it easier to transport and place, though it remained a hazardous explosive. The blasting cap was a separate invention. It made tunnels, mines, canals and harbours far cheaper to build.
- Pitfalls:
  - This is the entry where a mistake kills the maker: the reaction heats itself and explodes if it is not kept cold, and traces of acid left in the oil make it decompose later.
  - Carrying or storing the liquid; whole factories, ships and Nobel's own brother were lost that way.
  - Thawing frozen dynamite by a fire; old sticks that 'sweat' oil are as dangerous as the liquid.
  - Thinking a flame or fuse alone will set it off reliably; it needs a detonator.
  - Handling it gives violent headaches; the same substance in tiny doses relieves angina.
- History: europe: 1846 Schönbein's guncotton; 1847 Sobrero makes nitroglycerin (Turin) and warns against using it; 1863–1865 Nobel's detonator; 1867 dynamite; 1875 blasting gelatine; americas: 1866–1869 – nitroglycerin used on the Central Pacific Railroad and the Hoosac Tunnel
- Read:
  - G. I. Brown, The Big Bang: A History of Explosives (1998)
  - Kenne Fant, Alfred Nobel: A Biography (1993)
